                               Affidavit of Robert R. Stephens

       Robert R. Stephens, being first duly sworn, on his oath states:

       1.      My name is Robert R. Stephens. I am a Senior Principal with Brubaker &
Associates, Inc., having its principal place of business at 16690 Swingley Ridge Road, Suite 140,
Chesterfield, Missouri 63017. We have been retained by the Regents of the New Mexico State
University in this proceeding on their behalf.

       2.      Attached hereto and made a part hereof for all purposes is my rebuttal testimony
prepared in written form for introduction into evidence in Docket No. 25-00082-UT.

       3.      I hereby swear and affirm that the testimony is true and correct and that it shows
the matters and things that it purports to show.

 1   Q   PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.

 2   A   Robert R. Stephens. My business address is 16690 Swingley Ridge Road,

 3       Suite 140, Chesterfield, MO 63017.



 4   Q   WHAT IS YOUR OCCUPATION?

 5   A   I am a consultant in the field of public utility regulation and a Senior

 6       Principal with the firm of Brubaker & Associates, Inc. (“BAI”), energy,

 7       economic and regulatory consultants.



 8   Q   ARE YOU THE SAME ROBERT R. STEPHENS WHO PRESENTED

 9       DIRECT TESTIMONY IN THIS PROCEEDING ON OCTOBER 23,

10       2026?

11   A   Yes, I am.



12   Q   ON WHOSE BEHALF ARE YOU APPEARING IN THIS

13       PROCEEDING?

14   A   I am appearing on behalf of the Regents of the New Mexico State University

15       (“NMSU”).




                                       Page 1
                         Rebuttal Testimony of Robert R. Stephens
                           NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


1    Q   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR REBUTTAL TESTIMONY IN

2        THIS PROCEEDING?

3    A   In my rebuttal testimony, I will respond to the direct testimony of the

4        Coalition for Clean Affordable Energy (“CCAE”) witness Mr. Ron Nelson,

5        as it relates to generation cost allocation in the cost of service study.

6        Specifically, I address his recommendation that the Commission require

 7       El Paso Electric Company (“EPE” or “the Company”) to adopt the

 8       Probability of Dispatch (“POD”) method for generation cost allocation.



 9   Q   PLEASE SUMMARIZE YOUR REBUTTAL TESTIMONY.

10   A   My testimony can be summarized as follows:

11          Mr. Nelson’s recommendation to use POD should be rejected. It is not
12           a good measure of the classes’ contributions to the cost of EPE’s
13           generation system. EPE’s proposed classification and allocations are
14           more reasonable.

15          The POD methodology is a significant departure from the method that
16           the Company used to design its cost of service study in this proceeding
17           and from the methods accepted in New Mexico. Adopting POD would
18           require EPE to rerun its entire generation cost allocation using a
19           fundamentally different methodology and to produce a revised cost of
20           service study and revised class revenue allocations.

21          POD, as Mr. Nelson proposes it in this case, has not been approved by
22           any other public service commission in the US, despite his misleading
23           suggestions to the contrary.

24          As indicated by the single Colorado utility that received approval of a
25           different POD methodology, without peak hours, what Mr. Nelson


                                        Page 2
                         Rebuttal Testimony of Robert R. Stephens
                           NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


1            recommends “is essentially a 100 percent energy allocator and that class
2            cost responsibilities are changed so that the Residential customer class
3            sees a decline in cost responsibility that is inconsistent with energy
4            usage and growing peak demand.”

5           Other customers, particularly non-profit entities such as NMSU, are also
6            facing rising costs and affordability concerns. To deviate from class
7            cost of service principles and increase cross-class subsidization to
8            benefit one class over other classes is neither fair nor equitable.

 9          The Regulatory Assistance Project Manual, upon which Mr. Nelson
10           relies, even notes that the POD has limitations, including the fact that it
11           does not consider the reason that the investments were incurred, only
12           the way they are currently used, and that the POD allocation should be
13           based on weather-normalized dispatch and load, which adds significant
14           complexity to the calculation, and does not appear to have been
15           followed by Mr. Nelson.

16          In summary, the POD method has not been shown to have a history of
17           use in the utility industry, is overly complicated and, as such, would
18           diminish transparency in rate making. Most importantly, it violates cost
19           causation principles. It seriously undervalues capacity during peak
20           hours and effectively ignores what caused EPE to build its generation
21           fleet in the first place.

22          Despite Mr. Nelson’s protestations, the Average and Excess (“A&E”)
23           allocator used by EPE properly is based on capacity that is needed and
24           used to serve demand in every hour of the year, plus the additional
25           capacity that is used to serve demand only during the peak demand
26           periods that drive capacity additions.



27   Q   WHAT DOES CCAE WITNESS NELSON RECOMMEND AS IT

28       RELATES TO GENERATION COST ALLOCATION?

29   A   Mr. Nelson covers this at pages 85-98 of his direct testimony. In this

30       section, he claims that EPE’s Average and Excess (“A&E”) method does



                                         Page 3
                         Rebuttal Testimony of Robert R. Stephens
                           NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


1        not result in an equitable allocation of EPE’s non-peaking generation costs.

2        He lists some concerns with EPE’s proposed four coincident peak (“4CP”)

3        A&E method (“4CP-A&E”), calculates an alternative POD allocation, and

4        ultimately recommends that the Commission require EPE to perform a cost

5        of service study and apply the POD method for allocating the demand-

 6       related production costs to customer classes and prepare new revenue

7        apportionment and rate design proposals based on the new cost of service

8        results.



9    Q   DOES MR. NELSON PROVIDE ALTERNATIVE COST OF

10       SERVICE RESULTS USING THE POD METHOD?

11   A   Yes, but his position is curious and casts some doubt on his results. He

12       calculates alternative results in Table RN-2, shown on page 94 of his direct

13       testimony, and offers proposed class revenue apportionments at alleged cost

14       of service in Table RN-3 at page 96 of his direct testimony. However, he

15       ultimately recommends “that the Commission require the Company to

16       perform a CCOSS and apply the POD method for allocating the

17       demand-related production costs to customer classes and prepare new

18       revenue apportionment and rate design proposals based on the new CCOSS




                                        Page 4
                                Rebuttal Testimony of Robert R. Stephens
                                  NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1             results.”1 This is curious because although Mr. Nelson computed his own

 2             results, he does not explain what he would expect to be different if EPE

 3             calculated the analysis or why EPE would need to re-compute the results.

 4             This position casts some doubt on the accuracy of his calculations.



 5   Q         WHAT, IN MR. NELSON’S TESTIMONY, IS HIS CAUSAL

 6             JUSTIFICATION FOR USING THE POD?

 7   A          Mr. Nelson states his justification at page 97 indicating his belief that “POD

 8             more accurately reflects the costs caused by large loads and high-load factor

 9             customers, thereby better matching customer benefits with billing.”



10   Q         DO YOU AGREE THAT THE POD METHOD SHOULD BE USED

11             IN THIS CASE?

12   A          No.   Under the POD method, each generating unit’s annual revenue

13             requirement is assigned to the 8,760 hours of the year in proportion to that

14             unit’s hourly generation, and resulting hourly production revenue

15             requirement is then allocated to customer classes in proportion to each

16             class’s share of load in each hour. His POD analysis results, shown in

17             Table RN-2, would shift approximately 7% of revenue requirement



     1
         Nelson Direct Testimony at 97-98.


                                                Page 5
                                Rebuttal Testimony of Robert R. Stephens
                                  NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1              responsibility from the Residential class, and increases the percent

 2              responsibilities of the larger customer classes such as Large Power,

 3              Government/Military, New Mexico State University Rate 26, and

 4              Ag/Water/Sewer by 41%, 16%, 16%, and 15%, respectively. These are

 5              major differences.



 6   Q          DID YOUR DIRECT TESTIMONY ADDRESS THE GENERATION

 7              COST CLASSIFICATION AND ALLOCATION METHODOLOGY?

 8   A          Yes. In my direct testimony I reviewed the Company’s use of the 4CP

 9              classification and allocation methodology for peaking generating units and

10              its 4CP-A&E method for classifying and allocating the costs of non-peaking

11              units, and I concluded that these were consistent with cost causation and

12              appropriate for classifying and allocating EPE’s fixed production capacity

13              costs.2 EPE’s proposed method has been used by the Company in prior rate

14              cases, as indicated in EPE’s direct testimony.




     2
         Stephens Direct Testimony at 8-9.


                                               Page 6
                         Rebuttal Testimony of Robert R. Stephens
                           NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


1    Q   WHY DO YOU OPPOSE USE OF THE POD METHODOLOGY IN

2        THIS CASE?

3    A   There are multiple reasons. First, the POD methodology is a significant

4        departure from the method the Company used to design its cost of service

5        study in this proceeding, and from the methods accepted in New Mexico.

6        Adopting POD would require EPE to rerun its entire generation cost

7        allocation using a fundamentally different methodology and to produce a

8        revised cost of service study and revised class revenue allocations. This is

9        not a minor adjustment.

10              Second, POD is not widely used by electric utilities. Indeed, what

11       Mr. Nelson proposes in this case has not been approved by any other public

12       service commission in the US, despite his misleading suggestion to the

13       contrary.



14   Q   PLEASE EXPLAIN WHY YOU DISAGREE WITH MR. NELSON’S

15       ASSERTION IN THIS REGARD.

16   A   At pages 91-92, he claims that the POD method is used by other utilities,

17       citing Public Service Company of Colorado and Northern States Power

18       Wisconsin (“NSPW”). In the case of Public Service Company of Colorado,

19       as Mr. Nelson acknowledges, only the 1,000 highest load hours of the year

20       are used, making it significantly different from what he proposes here,


                                        Page 7
                              Rebuttal Testimony of Robert R. Stephens
                                NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1           because it limits the analysis to only 11% of the hours that Mr. Nelson

 2           would use.3 Use of 1,000 hours, though still not rendering the POD method

 3           as correct, at least acknowledges that the 89% of lower usage hours do not

 4           contribute significantly to the causality of the generation system.



 5   Q       HOW DID PUBLIC SERVICE COMPANY OF COLORADO

 6           DEFEND ITS POD-PEAK HOUR CHOICE OF LIMITING TO 1,000

 7           HOURS?

 8   A       The utility stated that if all hours were used, as in POD using all 8,760 hours

 9           of the year, the result would allocate costs during periods of low load when

10           renewable energy production could be curtailed.4

11                   The Colorado utility also “caution[ed] that the POD methodology,

12           without peak hours, is essentially a 100 percent energy allocator and that

13           class cost responsibilities are changed so that the Residential customer class

14           sees a decline in cost responsibility that is inconsistent with energy usage

15           and growing peak demand.”5 The Colorado Public Utilities Commission

16           approved the POD-Peak Hours approach.6



     3
       1,000/8,760 = 11.4%.
     4
       See, Decision No. C24-0117 of the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado,
     Proceeding No. 23AL-0243E, February 7, 2024, at 10.
     5

 1                  Unlike the POD-Peak Hours approach, Mr. Nelson’s version of

 2       POD utilizes all 8,760 hours, which yields different results. Accordingly,

 3       his proposal ultimately lacks precedential support from any other

 4       jurisdiction, and skews the results to favor Residential customers even

 5       further.     This skewed approach would be contrary to established and

 6       accepted class cost of service principles, and would harm not-for-profit

 7       customers such as NMSU, whose load is driven by the need to supply

 8       electricity to accomplish its teaching and research missions for the state.



 9   Q   DO YOU AGREE THAT MR. NELSON’S POD RESULTS WOULD

10       ESSENTIALLY AMOUNT TO A 100 PERCENT ENERGY

11       ALLOCATOR?

12   A   Yes. This is easily seen by comparing his results to a pure energy allocator,

13       as I show in Columns 3 and 4 in Table 1, below.

6    Q   WHAT ABOUT THE USE OF POD BY NSPW AS ALLEGED BY

7        MR. NELSON?

8    A   This is false. Despite Mr. Nelson’s characterization at page 92 of his direct

 9       testimony, including footnote 130, NSPW has only proposed that POD be

10       used, and only in a limited, special case, way. The case to which Mr. Nelson


                                                        Page 10
                            Rebuttal Testimony of Robert R. Stephens
                              NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1          refers is an Application related to approval of a Very Large General Time

 2          of Day Service Tariff.7 It is not in a general rate case and is not proposed

 3          to be used for an allocation of the overall system generation production

 4          costs, as Mr. Nelson would apply it here. Rather, in the Wisconsin case, it

 5          is proposed by NSPW to be used for the specific purpose of trying to isolate

 6          the costs of new very large load customers with demands that exceed

 7          100 MW in size.8 That is a very different use from what Mr. Nelson

 8          proposes.

 9                  Further, the NSPW Application indicates clearly that NSPW

10          proposes only to add POD the five traditional class cost of service methods,

11          utilizing four separate production cost allocation methods, which it

12          describes in Table 7 of the Application, not replace them with POD.9

13                  Perhaps more importantly, use of POD in Wisconsin is far from

14          established. The case to which Mr. Nelson refers is only in the early stages,

15          with direct testimony of Wisconsin intervenors and Commission Staff not

16          even due until December 11, 2026 and an order in the case not expected

17          until after February 2027.10 Thus, Mr. Nelson’s claim that “Northern States

 1           Power Wisconsin is also using the POD approach” is highly misleading as

 2           it is far from approved.



 3   Q       DESPITE ITS LACK OF USE, IS POD LISTED IN THE “ELECTRIC

 4           UTILITY COST ALLOCATION MANUAL” PUBLISHED BY THE

 5           NATIONAL         ASSOCIATION            OF    REGULATORY             UTILITY

 6           COMMISSIONERS (“NARUC MANUAL”)?

 7   A       Yes.    However, the NARUC Manual identifies several challenges

 8           associated with its use, which may explain in part why it is not adopted by

 9           public service commissions, save the single instance of a modified

10           version.11 Further, I would note that among the many different production

11           allocation methods illustrated with results in the NARUC Manual, as shown

12           at Table 4-18 of the Manual, POD is not included.



13   Q       WHAT ARE SOME OF THE CRITICISMS OF THE POD

14           METHOD?

15   A       In pushing for POD, in at least one state, Mr. Nelson has cited an alternative

16           cost of service manual published by the Regulatory Assistance Project



     11
       According to the NARUC Manual at page 62, “It must be noted that this method has
     substantial input data and analysis requirements that may make it prohibitively expensive
     for utilities that do not develop and maintain the required data.”


                                             Page 12
                             Rebuttal Testimony of Robert R. Stephens
                               NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1          (“RAP”), which does describe the POD method.12 This RAP Manual,

2           authored by residential advocate consultants, is often cited by residential

3           advocates in cost of service matters. Mr. Nelson refers to it in this case as

4           well, at page 13, footnote 9. However, even the RAP Manual notes that the

5           POD has limitations, including the fact that it does not consider the reason

 6          that the investments were incurred, only the way they are currently used.

 7          That is, it is only the current use, not historical causation.13

 8                  Another criticism in the RAP Manual is that the POD allocation

 9          should be based on weather-normalized dispatch and load, which adds

10          significantly complexity to the calculation, and does not appear to have been

11          followed by Mr. Nelson.14

12                  Despite Mr. Nelson’s claims that POD would more accurately

13          allocate generation costs,15 I wholly disagree that it is appropriate for this

14          case or that it should be given serious consideration in determining the

15          revenue allocation decision by the Commission. It has not been shown to

16          have a history of use in the utility industry, is overly complicated and, as

 2              violates cost causation principles. It seriously undervalues capacity during

 4              fleet in the first place.



 5   Q          DO YOU HAVE OTHER CONCERNS ABOUT THE USE OF THE

 6              POD METHOD?

 7   A          Yes.    As mentioned, Mr. Nelson’s POD method produces a large

 8              reallocation of generation cost responsibility onto customer classes other

 9              than Residential, including Large Power customers, Government and

10              Military customers, and New Mexico State University.16           These are

11              established customers, many of whom have taken service on the Company’s

12              system for years, and have made significant operational and investment

13              decisions in reliance on prior price signals. Under Mr. Nelson’s proposal,

14              these customers would face increased generation cost responsibility, not

15              because their usage patterns have changed, but because the production cost

16              allocator has changed.




     16
          Nelson Direct Testimony at 94, Table RN-2.


                                                Page 14
                                 Rebuttal Testimony of Robert R. Stephens
                                   NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1   Q           MR. NELSON CRITICIZES EPE’S A&E METHOD, CLAIMING

 2               THAT IT IS AN OUTDATED MEASURE OF PRODUCTION COST

 3               CAUSATION THAT PLACES TOO MUCH EMPHASIS ON PEAK

 4               DEMAND,17 AND THAT EVALUATING THE FULL 8,760 HOURLY

 5               LOAD PROFILES AND THEIR SUBSEQUENT COST IMPACT ON

 6               THE COMPANY’S PRODUCTION COST IS ESPECIALLY

 7               IMPORTANT         BECAUSE        OF      THE    GROWING        ROLE        OF

 8               RENEWABLES AND STORAGE.18 DO YOU AGREE?

 9   A           No. Mr. Nelson’s critique conflates two distinct questions: (1) whether the

10               allocator correctly identifies the capacity portion of the production cost

11               function, and (2) whether the allocator reflects every hourly dispatch

12               decision in a changing resource portfolio. The A&E method is designed to

13               answer the first question, and it does not purport to answer the second.

14                      The A&E method allocates fixed production capacity costs. Those

15               costs are incurred to ensure that sufficient capacity is available to serve

16               system peak demand reliably. The method decomposes system capacity

17               into two non-overlapping components, the capacity needed to serve average

18               demand, which is allocated on energy, and the incremental "excess"

19               capacity needed to serve load above average up to the system peak, which


     17
          Id. at 87.
     18
          Id. at 89.


                                                Page 15
                     Rebuttal Testimony of Robert R. Stephens
                       NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1   is allocated on the class contribution to peak. Mr. Nelson’s suggestion that

 2   the method places too much emphasis on a few peak hours is misplaced.

 3   The A&E allocator is based on capacity that is needed and used to serve

 4   demand in every hour of the year, plus the additional capacity that is used

 5   to serve demand only during the peak demand periods that drive capacity

 6   additions.

 7          The increasing share of renewables and storage does not change the

 8   fundamental driver of fixed production capacity investment. Even in a

 9   portfolio with substantial renewables and storage, the utility must plan for

10   a quantity of firm, dispatchable capacity able to serve demand reliably in all

11   hours, and that quantity is driven by peak and net-peak reliability

12   conditions. All else equal, as the system adds more renewable resources

13   with effectively zero energy cost, the fixed capital costs of the firm

14   resources that back up those renewables become a larger share of total

15   production cost, and those fixed costs are incurred specifically to meet peak

16   and net-peak reliability requirements. In a renewables-heavy system, the

17   case for allocating fixed capacity costs on a peak demand-related basis

18   becomes stronger, not weaker. An allocator that re-allocates those fixed

19   costs across all 8,760 hours based on hourly dispatch outcomes produces

20   worse price signals, not better ones.




                                    Page 16
                                Rebuttal Testimony of Robert R. Stephens
                                  NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1   Q          MR. NELSON ASSERTS THAT CUSTOMER CLASSES WITH

 2              HIGH      LOAD      FACTORS        WHICH       OPERATE       SIMILARLY

 3              AROUND THE CLOCK AND YEAR BECOME EXTREMELY

 4              EXPENSIVE TO SERVE BECAUSE THEY WILL REQUIRE MORE

 5              STORAGE AND DISPATCHABLE RESOURCES.19                           DO YOU

 6              AGREE?

 7   A          No. That assertion inverts the traditional understanding of cost causation

 8              for fixed production capacity, and it depends entirely on the choice of

 9              allocation method as the baseline. The A&E method measures each class’s

10              contribution to the need for capacity, whereas POD measures each class’s

11              consumption weighted by the cost of the hours in which that consumption

12              occurs. A class that uses energy relatively steadily across the year, as the

13              higher load factor customers do, will generally have a lower unit capacity

14              cost under A&E because steady load reflects efficient utilization of the

15              capacity the utility must build, but a higher unit cost under POD because

16              steady load means consumption during both low-cost and high-cost hours.

17              High load factor is a sign of efficient use of the system, not a reason to

18              assign these customers a disproportionate share of fixed capacity cost.




     19
          Nelson Direct Testimony at 89-90.


                                               Page 17
                         Rebuttal Testimony of Robert R. Stephens
                           NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


1    Q   AT    PAGE      83,    MR.     NELSON        TESTIFIES       THAT      THE

2        TRADITIONAL COST CAUSATION LOGIC HAS BEEN THAT

3        CUSTOMERS WITH HIGHER PEAK DEMAND INCURRED

4        GREATER COSTS FOR GENERATION TRANSMISSION AND

5        DISTRIBUTION          INFRASTRUCTURE,              BUT     THAT       THIS

 6       PERSPECTIVE EXCLUDES CONSIDERATION OF ENERGY USE

 7       AS A FACTOR IN COST CAUSATION AND COST ALLOCATION

 8       FOR FIXED GENERATION COSTS. HOW DO YOU RESPOND?

9    A   The A&E method proposed by EPE includes consideration of energy use as

10       a factor in cost causation and cost allocation, through the “average” demand

11       component which is essentially an energy allocator, and which determines

12       the allocation of a significant portion of the cost, equal to the system load

13       factor. Consequently, Mr. Nelson's criticism here is misplaced as it relates

14       to EPE’s proposed 4CP-A&E allocation.




                                        Page 18
                         Rebuttal Testimony of Robert R. Stephens
                           NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


1    Q   AT PAGE 88, MR. NELSON CLAIMS, “BECAUSE THE A&E

2        METHOD         WEIGHTS          ITS      AVERAGE          AND      EXCESS

3        COMPONENTS BY THE SYSTEM LOAD FACTOR, A DECLINING

4        LOAD      FACTOR        SHIFTS      MORE       WEIGHT        ONTO       THE

 5       PEAK-DEMAND COMPONENT OF THE 4CP-A&E ALLOCATOR,

 6       COMPOUNDING THE OVER-EMPHASIS ON PEAK DEMAND

 7       DESCRIBED ABOVE.” HOW DO YOU RESPOND?

 8   A   Mr. Nelson has it backwards. As load factor declines, this means that

 9       peaking needs are a greater contributor to the need for resources and,

10       accordingly, more weight should be placed on the peak-demand component.

11       This is illustrated readily by considering the extreme case of a 100% load

12       factor system, with all load operating at exactly the same level in all hours.

13       In that case, peaking needs would essentially be non-existent and the cause

14       of generation cost would be primarily energy-related. This is exactly how

15       an A&E allocator works, with the average demand, or energy, being

16       weighted by the system load factor. Conversely, consider a hypothetical

17       system with load of zero in all hours except a single hour of demand spike.

18       In this case, the system load factor would approach zero, and an A&E

19       allocation would be fully weighted on demand – an appropriate indication
